KV cache entries represent the precomputed attention keys and values for each token; evicting one means recomputing it later at non-trivial cost, so eviction policy directly trades GPU memory against latency and throughput. In the single-request case, eviction is a local decision: you're managing one timeline of tokens and LRU or recency-weighted policies are at least coherent. With prefix-sharing across concurrent requests—as implemented in systems like vLLM's prefix caching and SGLang's RadixAttention—the KV cache becomes a shared trie-indexed structure, and evicting a node invalidates it for every in-flight or future request that shares that prefix, turning a local memory decision into a global coordination problem. The reuse value of a cache entry is now a function of fan-out: a shared system prompt seen by 1,000 concurrent requests is catastrophically expensive to evict compared to a unique user-specific suffix, but a standard LRU policy cannot distinguish these because it only sees recency, not reference count or branching factor in the trie. SGLang's RadixAttention paper (Zheng et al., 2023) demonstrated cache hit rate improvements of 20–40% over vLLM's simpler prefix caching precisely because it tracks the tree structure and can make eviction decisions at the node level rather than the flat token level. The expert concern is trie depth vs. breadth asymmetry: a deep, narrow chain (long unique context) looks equally "hot" to a shallow, wide node (short shared prefix with many dependents) if you only track access recency, so you can end up evicting a node that serves 500 requests to keep one that serves 1—a policy inversion that worsens under load precisely when you can least afford it. Fixing this requires reference-count-weighted or marginal-reuse-value scoring, which adds bookkeeping overhead and introduces contention on the metadata itself at high request rates.

Reactive re-warming's central failure mode is the cold-start latency spike: the window between shift detection and cache repopulation forces every request to pay full prefill cost, and at 100K-token contexts on H100s, prefill for a single request can run 2–5 seconds—meaning even a 30-second re-warming window translates to hundreds of requests absorbing multi-second first-token latencies simultaneously, which can cascade into queue buildup that outlasts the re-warming itself. A subtler reactive failure is eviction thrashing during re-warming: to populate the new prefix pattern, you must prefill it, which generates new KV entries that compete for the same memory budget currently occupied by the old pattern's entries—if you evict the old pattern aggressively to make room, in-flight requests still using the old pattern pay recompute cost; if you evict conservatively, re-warming stalls and the new pattern never achieves steady-state hit rate. Proactive pinning fails differently: it requires a correct prediction of the incoming prefix, and pinning the wrong prefix wastes reserved memory budget that could have served actual traffic—in a memory-constrained system (typical GPU KV cache utilization runs 70–90% in production), pinning even 10–15% of capacity for a mispredicted prefix can push the system into the eviction-thrashing regime anyway. Proactive pinning also introduces priority inversion under prediction error: pinned entries are by definition protected from eviction, so when the prediction is wrong, the system is forced to evict high-reuse unpinned entries to serve live traffic while holding useless pinned entries—this is strictly worse than reactive re-warming because at least reactive strategies evict based on observed signal. Between the two, proactive pinning is more dangerous in latency-sensitive environments: reactive re-warming produces a bounded, detectable latency spike that resolves as the cache warms, whereas a mispredicted pin creates a persistent memory tax with no self-correcting mechanism until the pin is explicitly released, and the conditions that cause misprediction (non-stationary traffic) are exactly the conditions where you're least likely to notice and correct it quickly.

The theoretically grounded approach is to set steady-state utilization target based on transition cost amortization: if a full pattern shift requires prefilling N tokens of new prefix content, and your recompute budget per request is B tokens before latency SLOs break, then headroom should be at least N/total_cache_capacity—for a 32K shared system prompt on a 512K-token cache, that's ~6% headroom minimum, but real deployments should 2–3x that to absorb concurrent in-flight requests still using the old pattern, landing around 15–20% free capacity as a practical floor. The asymmetry that experts track is that over-utilization failures are acute and visible (latency spikes, SLO violations, queue buildup) while under-utilization failures are chronic and invisible (reduced throughput, higher cost-per-token, unnecessary scale-out)—monitoring systems almost universally instrument the former and ignore the latter, so production systems drift toward over-utilization because that's where the pager fires. The correct answer is a dynamic target that adjusts based on observed traffic entropy: low-entropy traffic (one dominant prefix) can safely run at 85%+ because transitions are rare and predictable; high-entropy traffic (many competing prefixes) should target 65–70% because the effective working set is large and pattern shifts are frequent—but almost no production serving system implements this today, defaulting instead to a single static threshold.

In single-tenant systems, eviction cost is internalized—the same workload that causes eviction pays the recompute penalty—which creates at least a loose alignment between policy and consequence. In multi-tenant or multi-model serving, this alignment breaks entirely: a burst from Tenant A that fills the cache forces eviction of Tenant B's entries, but Tenant B pays the recompute latency while Tenant A's requests complete fast, creating a cost externalization problem that is structurally identical to network congestion externalities and requires similar solutions—either isolation or chargeback mechanisms. Systems like Orca and more recently Tetris (Microsoft, 2024) address this through cache partitioning with soft reservations: each tenant gets a guaranteed minimum cache partition that cannot be evicted by other tenants, plus access to a shared overflow pool, trading some efficiency (reserved capacity sits idle during low-tenant-load periods) for fairness and predictability. The multi-model case is worse than multi-tenant because model weight memory and KV cache memory compete for the same HBM pool, and a model swap—loading a new model's weights—can force wholesale KV cache eviction across all tenants simultaneously; this is the core operational problem that systems like Punica and S-LoRA tried to solve for LoRA adapters by keeping base model weights resident and only swapping small adapter weights, reducing but not eliminating the eviction blast radius. The accountability gap that no deployed system handles well is causal attribution: when Tenant B's p99 latency spikes because Tenant A's burst evicted its cache entries, standard metrics show Tenant B's latency degraded but don't expose the cross-tenant eviction as root cause—operators see a symptom in one tenant's dashboard with the cause buried in another's memory pressure metrics, making SLO contracts for cached inference latency essentially unenforceable in shared clusters today.

To price recompute externalities accurately, each cache entry would need to carry: origin tenant ID, entry creation cost in FLOPs or wall-clock prefill time, reference count and fan-out (how many requests have used this entry since insertion), eviction cause (which tenant's allocation pressure triggered it), and counterfactual recompute cost—the prefill FLOPs that would be incurred if a future request needed this entry and found it missing, which requires predicting future access probability at eviction time. The counterfactual cost is the fundamental hard problem: you need to estimate P(this entry will be accessed again | current traffic state) at the moment of eviction, which is exactly the cache hit rate prediction problem, and getting it wrong in either direction means either over-charging the evicting tenant (chilling legitimate bursts) or under-charging them (failing to deter externality-generating behavior). The metadata overhead is non-trivial: tracking per-entry tenant attribution, creation cost, and access history adds roughly 100–200 bytes of metadata per cache entry, and at 100K-token contexts with 32 attention heads and fp16 KV pairs, a single entry already consumes megabytes—so metadata is small relatively but at millions of entries across a cluster, the aggregated bookkeeping state becomes a distributed systems problem requiring consistent reads across nodes at microsecond decision timescales. The causal attribution problem is worse than it appears because eviction is often a chain reaction: Tenant A's burst evicts Tenant B's entry, which forces Tenant B to recompute, which generates new cache entries that evict Tenant C's entries—assigning cost to the originating tenant requires tracing an eviction cascade graph in real time, which no current system does and which would require something like distributed tracing infrastructure (analogous to Dapper/Jaeger) applied to memory management events. The deepest obstacle is temporal mismatch: the eviction decision happens in microseconds during request scheduling, but the recompute cost materializes hundreds of milliseconds later during prefill, and the tenant responsible for the eviction may have already completed their requests and closed their billing window—making real-time chargeback require either speculative cost reservation (complex, error-prone) or retroactive billing adjustments (operationally messy and contractually fraught with enterprise customers expecting predictable inference costs).

The most tractable proxy is tenant-level cache pressure delta: rather than tracking per-entry eviction causality, you measure each tenant's instantaneous cache footprint as a fraction of total capacity, and when total utilization exceeds threshold, you attribute recompute cost proportionally to tenants whose footprint increased in the window preceding the eviction event—this is wrong in individual cases but unbiased in expectation over thousands of events, making it reasonable for billing aggregated over hourly or daily windows. A second useful proxy is eviction-rate-weighted prefill cost: for each tenant, track (evictions caused per unit time) × (average entry creation cost in that tenant's traffic), which can be computed entirely from per-tenant aggregate statistics without per-entry causal chains—Microsoft's AzureML serving telemetry reportedly uses a similar heuristic for internal cost attribution of shared GPU resources, though the specific implementation isn't public. Validation without intentional degradation is the genuinely hard part, and the best approach is shadow accounting with natural experiments: run the attribution proxy in logging-only mode and wait for organic traffic events—tenant onboarding, traffic spikes, model updates—that naturally perturb cache pressure, then compare the proxy's attributed costs against observed p99 prefill latency changes in affected tenants to check whether high-attribution periods correlate with high recompute latency; this requires no controlled degradation but demands 4–8 weeks of data collection to accumulate enough natural variance. A complementary validation technique is cross-tenant lag correlation: if your proxy correctly identifies Tenant A as causing externalities on Tenant B, then Tenant B's prefill latency should spike with a lag of one scheduling cycle (microseconds to milliseconds) after Tenant A's cache footprint surges—measuring this lag correlation across historical traces lets you compute a proxy precision-recall curve against observed latency events as ground truth without any deliberate harm. The fundamental validation limit is that proxies can be empirically good on historical traffic and still fail on new prompt structures, because the relationship between cache pressure and recompute cost is mediated by prefix-sharing topology that changes with traffic composition—so validation should include explicit stress-testing against held-out traffic segments with structurally different prompt patterns, which is synthetic but doesn't require degrading production tenant experience.
